The AI is told to use these and nothing else, so add per-bone facts under `structures` only from the paper or the Dryad README, never from memory. Bone name, side and source file are added automatically from the manifest.

specimen.text: Eosphorosuchus lacrimosa is an early crocodylomorph (an early relative of crocodiles) from the Late Triassic of Ghost Ranch, New Mexico.
Its skull differs from other early crocodylomorphs, including Hesperosuchus agilis, the species it had earlier been tentatively assigned to.
The researchers describe its facial region as unusually short and reinforced by bone.
The study's authors describe a short snout, a heavily reinforced skull and enlarged jaw muscles suited to snapping shut on large prey.
It lived about 210 million years ago and is described as a fast-running land predator that lived near rivers and lakes.

It was found in the same fossil assemblage as Hesperosuchus agilis. The researchers read their different skulls and jaws as a sign that closely related predators were already dividing up food resources with different feeding strategies.
The holotype, YPM VP 41198 at the Yale Peabody Museum, includes parts of the skull, lower jaw, vertebrae, limbs and armor.
The team's phylogenetic analysis places Eosphorosuchus near the base of Crocodylomorpha.
The species was identified using CT scans of a decades-old museum specimen, which let the team study bones still enclosed in rock and separate the skull elements digitally.
The name refers to Eosphoros, the 'dawn-bringer', pointing to the dawn of crocodylomorph ecological diversity; 'suchus' comes from the Greek word for crocodile.
specimen.source: Etymology from the paper, quoted by NovaTaxa (April 2026)

specimen.text: The 3D bone models in this viewer come from Appendix 2 of the authors' Dryad dataset, which holds 3D meshes of the skull elements extracted from the micro-CT scan; Appendix 1 holds the scan itself.
